metadata.scope: e_siberia (139 baronies across k_ob, k_sibir, k_yugra)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_chulym_bis.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Chulym River basin was inhabited by pre-literate Samoyedic, Yeniseian, and later Turkic (Chulym Tatar) groups until Russian documentation in the late 16th–17th centuries.

morphemes.translation: Chulym River (etymology uncertain; possibly from Turkic *čul/*čöl or Samoyedic substrate)

b_chulym_bis.etymology_analysis: The repo form 'Nider-Tschulîm' prefixes a Germanic-style 'Nider-' ('lower') locator to the Siberian hydronym Chulym (Russian Чулым), a major right tributary of the Ob in Krasnoyarsk Krai and Tomsk Oblast.

b_chet.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Chet River (right tributary of the Kiya) was first recorded in Russian Siberian hydrography and cartography after the late 16th-century conquest of Siberia.

morphemes.translation: river/stream (substrate hydronym in the Chulym-Kiya basin)

b_chet.etymology_analysis: Named after the Chet River (Russian Четь), a 432 km right tributary of the Kiya in Krasnoyarsk Krai and Tomsk Oblast; the hydronym reflects an indigenous Yeniseian or Samoyedic substrate.

b_shurysh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; appears to be a truncated or transferred CK3 form of Shuryshkary (first documented in Russian sources in the 17th–18th centuries on the lower Ob) or a synthetic Siberian barony name.
b_shurysh.etymology_analysis: Likely a truncated CK3 adaptation of Shuryshkary (Khanty 'town on the stream/channel'), a settlement on the lower Ob, though placed in the Chulym basin in-game; unattested in medieval written sources.

b_kiia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kiya River (left tributary of the Chulym) was first documented in Russian Siberian records in the 17th century.
b_kiia.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kiya River (Russian Кия), a 548 km left tributary of the Chulym flowing through Kemerovo and Tomsk Oblasts.

b_krolu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym in the Kiya basin.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_krolu.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Kiya county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_kitat.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kitat River (left tributary of the Yaya) was first recorded in Russian Siberian cartography in the 17th–18th centuries.
b_kitat.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kitat River (Russian Китат, formerly Mazalovsky Kitat), a left tributary of the Yaya in Kemerovo and Tomsk Oblasts, containing the Yeniseian hydronymic element *-tat* ('river').

b_kojuk.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kozhukh River (left tributary of the Kiya) was first documented in Russian Siberian records after the late 16th century.

morphemes.translation: fur coat / sheepskin coat (Russian folk-etymological adaptation of a local Turkic/Yeniseian hydronym)

b_kojuk.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to the Kozhukh River (Russian Кожух), a 144 km left tributary of the Kiya in Kemerovo Oblast.

b_biriku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Berikul River and settlement in Kemerovo Oblast were documented only after Russian colonization in the 17th–19th centuries.
b_biriku.etymology_analysis: Represents Berikul (Russian Берикуль), a river (tributary of the Kiya) and historic village in Kemerovo Oblast, from a Siberian Turkic compound.

b_narim.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1596 CE as Narymsky ostrog by Russian Cossacks from Surgut at the confluence of the Ob and Ket rivers.
b_narim.etymology_analysis: Narym (Russian Нарым) was founded in 1596 as a Russian ostrog; its name derives from Southern Selkup *nyar* ('swamp, marsh'), reflecting the surrounding Vasyugan-Ob wetlands.

b_tym.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tym River (right tributary of the Ob) was first recorded in Russian Siberian sources after the 1590s.
b_tym.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tym River (Russian Тым), a 950 km right tributary of the Ob in Krasnoyarsk Krai and Tomsk Oblast.

b_keljiga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym in the Narym/Tym region.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_keljiga.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Narym county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_yutur.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Narym county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_sochur.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Sochur River (right tributary of the Ket) was first recorded in Russian Siberian hydrography in the 17th century or later.
b_sochur.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sochur River (Russian Сочур), a 301 km right tributary of the Ket in Krasnoyarsk Krai.

b_jorugul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_jorugul.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Sochur county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_taskyl.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; 'Taskyl' is a regional Shor and Khakas common-noun orographic term for a bare alpine peak (goltsy) in the Kuznetsk Alatau, documented only in post-17th-century Russian and Turkic sources.
b_taskyl.etymology_analysis: From the Shor/Khakas common-noun topographic term *taskyl* ('bald peak, mountain tundra'), used in compounds across the Kuznetsk Alatau (e.g., Amzas-Taskyl, Bolshoy Taskyl).

b_perasku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_perasku.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Taskyl county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_yogoran.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_yogoran.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Taskyl county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_tomsk.first_mention_attestation: Tomsk was founded in 1604 CE by decree of Tsar Boris Godunov after Toyan, duke of the Eushta Tatars, requested Russian protection.

morphemes.translation: Eushta Tatar tribal/village name (repo form Eûschte)

b_tomsk.etymology_analysis: Tomsk was founded in 1604 on the Tom River near the Eushta Tatar settlement (represented by the repo's localized name 'Eûschte'). Both the -sk settlement name and the Eushta ethnonym are post-867 in written records.

b_ket.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Russian forces established Ketsk fort on the Ket River in 1602 CE.

morphemes.translation: river hydronym (cf. Ket *ket* 'person/human' or substrate river name)

b_ket.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ket River (Russian Кеть), a 1,621 km right tributary of the Ob in Krasnoyarsk Krai and Tomsk Oblast, which served as a major Siberian river route from 1602 onward.

b_salim.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Bolshoy Salym River (left tributary of the Ob) was first documented in Russian Siberian sources in the 17th–18th centuries.

morphemes.translation: river hydronym (Bolshoy Salym, left tributary of the Ob)

b_salim.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to the Salym (Bolshoy Salym) River, a 583 km left tributary of the Ob in Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug.

b_yaia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Yaya River (left tributary of the Chulym) was first documented in Russian Siberian records after the 17th century.

morphemes.translation: summer (possibly related to Turkic *yay* 'summer', or indigenous substrate)

b_yaia.etymology_analysis: Named after the Yaya River (Russian Яя), a 380 km left tributary of the Chulym flowing through Kemerovo and Tomsk Oblasts.

b_yenisei.first_mention_attestation: The Russian/Evenki form 'Yenisei' (via Evenki *Ioanesi* 'great water') is attested only from the early 17th-century Russian expansion (Yeniseysk ostrog founded in 1619 CE); earlier <= 867 CE sources record the river as 'Jian Shui' / 'Käm'.

morphemes.translation: great water / big river (adapted into Russian as Енисей)

b_yenisei.etymology_analysis: The modern name Yenisei (Russian Енисей) derives from Evenki *Ioanesi* ('great water') and entered written Russian records in the early 17th century (Yeniseysk founded 1619 CE). In pre-867 CE Chinese and Old Turkic sources, the upper river was known as Jian Shui / Käm.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Book of Zhou (636 CE, vol. 50) as Jian Shui (劍水); Old Turkic Orkhon inscriptions (8th century CE) as Käm
older_name_by_867.notes: Pre-867 CE Chinese Tang-era chronicles and 8th-century Orkhon inscriptions attest the upper Yenisei under the name Kem/Käm (transcribed Jian Shui/Jian He).

b_yahtin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym in the Yenisei region.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_yahtin.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Yenisei county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_belska.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the village of Belskoye in Krasnoyarsk Krai is documented in 19th-century Russian records (e.g., 1866 CE, place of exile of M. V. Butashevich-Petrashevsky).
b_belska.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to Belskoye (Russian Бельское), a Russian-era village in Pirovsky District, Krasnoyarsk Krai, west of the Yenisei.

b_igaran.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name in the Baraba Steppe with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_igaran.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Baraba Steppe with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_iau.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Igaran county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_chegarka.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Shegarka River (left tributary of the Ob in Novosibirsk and Tomsk Oblasts) was first documented in Russian Siberian sources after the 17th century.
b_chegarka.etymology_analysis: Represents the Shegarka River (Russian Шегарка), a left tributary of the Ob in Novosibirsk and Tomsk Oblasts; the name derives from Southern Selkup *Tagar/Chagar* with the Russian *-ka* suffix.

b_kolyvan.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1822 CE on the site of the 1713 Chaus ostrog in Novosibirsk Oblast.

morphemes.translation: historical Russian name transferred from Kolyvan Governorate (1782) / Tallinn

b_kolyvan.etymology_analysis: Kolyvan in Novosibirsk Oblast was founded in 1822 on the site of the Chaus fortress (1713), reusing the name of the earlier Kolyvan Viceroyalty/Governorate.

b_chik.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Chik River (tributary of the Oyosh) and the settlement of Chik in Novosibirsk Oblast were documented only in the Russian/modern period.

morphemes.translation: damp, wet, or narrow stream (hydronym in the Ob-Chik basin)

b_chik.etymology_analysis: Named after the Chik River (Russian Чик), a 114 km river in Novosibirsk Oblast that also gave its name to the urban-type settlement of Chik.

b_kayask.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kainsk (modern Kuybyshev in Novosibirsk Oblast) was founded in 1722 CE as a Russian fort (Kainsky pas / ostrog) in the Baraba Steppe.
b_kayask.etymology_analysis: Likely represents Kainsk (Russian Каинск, modern Kuybyshev), founded in 1722 in the Baraba Steppe and named with the Russian *-sk* suffix from Turkic *kayïn* ('birch').

b_karas_SIB.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Karasuk River in Novosibirsk Oblast was first documented in Russian sources in the 18th century.
b_karas_SIB.etymology_analysis: Derived from the Karasuk River (Russian Карасук) in Novosibirsk Oblast, from Turkic *kara su* ('black/spring-fed water').

b_konda_ob.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Konda River (left tributary of the Irtysh) and Kondia region entered Russian written records in the 15th–16th centuries.

morphemes.translation: Ob River (locator prefix in repo form Ôbkônde)
Konda River (cf. Mansi *Konda*, possibly 'pine' or 'long river')

b_konda_ob.etymology_analysis: The repo form 'Ôbkônde' is a compound locator combining 'Ob' and 'Konda' (Russian Конда, a 1,097 km left tributary of the Irtysh in Khanty-Mansia).

b_toya.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Toya River (tributary of the Baksa in Novosibirsk and Tomsk Oblasts) was first documented in Russian cartography after the 17th century.

morphemes.translation: river hydronym in the Ob-Shegarka-Baksa basin

b_toya.etymology_analysis: Named after the Toya River (Russian Тоя), a tributary of the Baksa (as well as another Toya tributary of the Chaya) in Novosibirsk and Tomsk Oblasts.

b_sartlan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lake Sartlan in the Baraba Steppe was first documented in Russian Siberian surveys from the 18th century onward.
b_sartlan.etymology_analysis: Named after Lake Sartlan (Russian Сартлан), a 238 km² endorheic hyposaline lake in the Baraba Steppe of Novosibirsk Oblast.

b_bagan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Bagan River in Novosibirsk Oblast was first documented in Russian sources from the 18th century onward.
b_bagan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bagan River (Russian Баган), a 364 km river in the southern Baraba Steppe of Novosibirsk Oblast.

b_chulym.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the settlement of Chulym (named after the Chulym River) was founded in 1762.

morphemes.translation: river hydronym (Baraba Steppe / Malye Chany basin)

b_chulym.etymology_analysis: Named after the Chulym River (Russian Чулым) in the endorheic Malye Chany basin of Novosibirsk Oblast, which also gave its name to the town of Chulym (founded 1762).

b_ubins.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ubinskoye (Ubinsky ostrog) in the Baraba Steppe was founded in the late 17th–early 18th century (c. 1675–1722 CE).
b_ubins.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to Ubinskoye (Russian Убинское) in Novosibirsk Oblast, named after Lake Ubinskoye with the Russian *-inskoye* settlement suffix.

b_kargat.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kargat River (right tributary of the Chulym) was first documented in Russian sources in the 18th century.
b_kargat.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kargat River (Russian Каргат), a 387 km right tributary of the Chulym in Novosibirsk Oblast, from Turkic *karagat* ('black currant').

b_baksa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Baksa River (right tributary of the Shegarka) was first documented in Russian Siberian hydrography in the 17th–18th centuries.

morphemes.translation: river hydronym in the Shegarka-Ob basin

b_baksa.etymology_analysis: Named after the Baksa River (Russian Бакса), a 206 km right tributary of the Shegarka flowing through Novosibirsk and Tomsk Oblasts.

b_tartas_SIB.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tartas River (right tributary of the Om) was first documented in Russian Siberian sources in the 17th–18th centuries (Ust-Tartassky ostrog built in the early 18th century).

morphemes.translation: river hydronym in the Om-Irtysh basin

b_tartas_SIB.etymology_analysis: Named after the Tartas River (Russian Тартас), a 566 km right tributary of the Om in Novosibirsk Oblast.

b_om.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Om River (right tributary of the Irtysh) entered Russian written records in the 17th–18th centuries.
b_om.etymology_analysis: Named after the Om River (Russian Омь), a 1,091 km right tributary of the Irtysh; the hydronym means 'quiet' in the Baraba Tatar dialect.

b_gulyus.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unverified CK3 barony name in the Vasyugan Mire with no identified real-world settlement or hydronym.

morphemes.translation: Unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name with no verified historical etymon

b_gulyus.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Tartas county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_chergana.etymology_analysis: Synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name placed in the Umiai county with no verified real-world Siberian toponymic match.

b_vasyugan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Vasyugan River (left tributary of the Ob) was first documented in Russian Siberian records after the late 16th century.
b_vasyugan.etymology_analysis: Named after the Vasyugan River (Russian Васюган), a 1,082 km left tributary of the Ob in Tomsk Oblast, containing the Khanty hydronymic element *yogan* ('river').

b_parabel.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Parabel River and selo of Parabel in Tomsk Oblast entered Russian records around 1600 CE when the village of Parabel was founded.

morphemes.translation: river hydronym (Russian Парабель; Narym Selkup name for the village is *Vargh kara*)

b_parabel.etymology_analysis: Named after the Parabel River (Russian Парабель), a 308 km left tributary of the Ob in Tomsk Oblast, and the selo of Parabel founded on it in 1600 CE.

b_yonoir.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name in the Vasyugan Mire.

morphemes.translation: Unattested CK3 barony name in the Vasyugan region

b_yonoir.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for the Vasyugan basin; appears to be a synthetic CK3 placeholder barony name.

b_yugar.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name in the Vasyugan Mire.

morphemes.translation: Unattested CK3 barony name (possibly modeled on Yugra)

b_yugar.etymology_analysis: No settlement named Yugar is attested in the Vasyugan region; likely a synthetic CK3 barony name loosely inspired by the regional exonym Yugra.

b_dolgujar.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1581 in accounts of Yermak's Siberian campaign (later recorded by G. F. Müller) as Dolgiy Yar on the Tobol River, the former name of Khudyakova in Tobolsky District, Tyumen Oblast.
b_dolgujar.etymology_analysis: From Russian Dolgiy Yar ('long steep bank/cliff'), referring to a high, elongated bank along the Tobol River near modern Khudyakova.

b_vagay.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1633 as Vagay ostrog/settlement in Tyumen Oblast; named after the Vagay River.

morphemes.translation: Hydronym of the Vagay River (etymology uncertain)

b_vagay.etymology_analysis: Named after the Vagay River, a left tributary of the Irtysh, whose hydronym is of indigenous Ob-Ugric or Siberian Tatar origin.

b_yalu_torovsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1639 (with the Russian sloboda of Yalutorovsky established in 1659) on the Tobol River in Tyumen Oblast.
b_yalu_torovsk.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation with the -ovsk settlement suffix of the earlier Siberian Tatar toponym Yavlu-Tura.

b_kurtan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern village of Kurtan in Mokrousovsky District, Kurgan Oblast, located on Lake Kurtan.
b_kurtan.etymology_analysis: Named after Lake Kurtan in the Tobol–Ishim interfluve (Kurgan Oblast), a hydronym of Turkic origin.

b_ishim.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1670 as Korkina Sloboda on the Ishim River and renamed Ishim upon receiving town status in 1782.
b_ishim.etymology_analysis: Named after the Ishim River (Kazakh Esil), a major left tributary of the Irtysh.

b_ust-ishim.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1631 as Ishimsky ostrog (Ust-Ishim) at the confluence of the Ishim and Irtysh rivers in Omsk Oblast.
b_ust-ishim.etymology_analysis: Russian locator compound meaning 'mouth of the Ishim', denoting the settlement at the confluence of the Ishim and Irtysh rivers.

b_omgul.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name in the Ishim region.
b_omgul.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for Western Siberia; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name.

b_vikulova.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in 1691 (and marked as Vikulova sloboda on Semyon Remezov's 1698 map) on the Ishim River in Tyumen Oblast.
b_vikulova.eponym_details: Named after a post-867 Russian settler bearing the personal name Vikul (Vikula) with the possessive suffix -ovo.
b_vikulova.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive settlement name derived from the personal name Vikul/Vikula plus the suffix -ovo/-ova.

b_astana.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1830 as the settlement of Akmoly (Akmolinsk in 1832) on the Ishim River; renamed Astana in 1998.
b_astana.etymology_analysis: From Kazakh astana meaning 'capital city' (ultimately from Persian āstāna 'threshold, royal court'), adopted in 1998; its medieval predecessor Bozok dates to the 12th–14th centuries.

b_erementau.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1948 during construction of the Akmola–Pavlodar railway in Akmola Region, Kazakhstan.
b_erementau.etymology_analysis: Named after the Yereymentau Mountains in northern Kazakhstan, containing Kazakh tau ('mountain').

b_dombraly.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern village in Akkol District, Akmola Region, Kazakhstan, named after the Dombraly mountain.
b_dombraly.etymology_analysis: Kazakh oronym and village name meaning 'having a dombra', associated in local legend with Mount Dombraly.

b_astrakhanka.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1889 (some sources cite 1892) by Russian settlers in Akmola Region, Kazakhstan.
b_astrakhanka.etymology_analysis: Russian colonial settlement name formed from Astrakhan (referring to settlers from Astrakhan Governorate) with the suffix -ka.

b_bulandy.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern village (formerly Zhalayyr) and district name in Akmola Region, Kazakhstan.

b_shchuchinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1850 as the Cossack settlement (vyselok) of Shchuchinskiy on Lake Shchuchye in Akmola Region, Kazakhstan.
b_shchuchinsk.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name with the -insk suffix derived from Lake Shchuchye ('Pike Lake').

b_koksengrisor.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; endorheic salt lake in Ualikhanov District, North Kazakhstan Region.
b_koksengrisor.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym for a salt lake in North Kazakhstan Region, composed of kök ('blue'), seŋgir ('ridge/height'), and sor ('salt lake/marsh').

b_seletyteniz.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; endorheic salt lake in North Kazakhstan Region.
b_seletyteniz.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym combining Sileti (the river feeding the basin) with teŋiz ('sea, large lake').

b_teke.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; bittern salt lake in Ualikhanov District, North Kazakhstan Region.
b_teke.etymology_analysis: Kazakh hydronym for Lake Teke in North Kazakhstan Region, from Kazakh teke ('billy-goat/ibex').

b_ertis.first_mention_attestation: No settlement, fortress, or administrative attestation <= 867 CE; the Old Turkic Tonyukuk inscription (c. 720 CE) records Ärtiš ügüz strictly as a hydronym (the Irtysh River), while the modern settlement of Ertis (Irtyshsk) in Pavlodar Region was founded in 1911.

morphemes.translation: Irtysh River (etymology debated; possibly Turkic or Yeniseian-Iranian)

b_ertis.etymology_analysis: Kazakh name (Ertis) of the Irtysh River, attested in Old Turkic as Ärtiš in the 8th-century Tonyukuk inscription.

b_karaoba.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; widespread Kazakh toponym (e.g., Karaoba in Pavlodar Region).
b_karaoba.etymology_analysis: Kazakh compound toponym meaning 'black mound/kurgan', formed from qara ('black') and oba ('mound, burial hill').

b_kainsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1722 as the military fort Kainsky Pas on the Om/Kainka River; granted town status as Kainsk in 1782 (renamed Kuybyshev in 1935).
b_kainsk.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name with the -sk suffix derived from the Kainka River (Turkic qayın 'birch').

b_chany.first_mention_attestation: Settlement founded in 1875 as Novopokrovskaya zaimka in Novosibirsk Oblast, later renamed Chany after Lake Chany.
b_chany.etymology_analysis: Named after Lake Chany (Siberian Tatar Tsana kül), derived from Turkic çan ('large vessel/tub').

b_abyszkan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Lake Abyshkan in the Baraba forest-steppe, Novosibirsk Oblast (formerly part of Lake Chany).
b_abyszkan.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of Lake Abyshkan in the Baraba steppe (Novosibirsk Oblast), of indigenous Siberian Tatar/Turkic origin.

b_karasuk.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the town of Karasuk in Novosibirsk Oblast was founded in the late 18th century (town status 1954), named after the Karasuk River.
b_karasuk.etymology_analysis: Named after the Karasuk River, a common Turkic hydronym meaning 'black water/spring-fed stream'.

b_omsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1716 as a Russian fortress at the confluence of the Om and Irtysh rivers by Ivan Buchholz.
b_omsk.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name with the -sk suffix derived from the Om River (from Baraba Tatar meaning 'quiet').

b_sals_poveret.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name in the Omsk area.
b_sals_poveret.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for the Omsk/Irtysh region; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name.

b_tiabis.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; modern Siberian Tatar aul of Tebis (Chüplekül) in Chanovsky District, Novosibirsk Oblast.
b_tiabis.etymology_analysis: Corresponds to the Baraba Tatar village of Tebis in Chanovsky District, Novosibirsk Oblast; no pre-867 documentary attestation exists.

b_tatarka.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1740 as a Cossack redoubt on the Irtysh River in Cherlaksky District, Omsk Oblast.
b_tatarka.etymology_analysis: Russian ethnonym-derived settlement name from Tatar with the -ka suffix.

b_pavlodar.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1720 as the Koryakovsky outpost on the Irtysh River and renamed Pavlodar in 1861.
b_pavlodar.eponym_details: Named Pavlodar ('Gift of Paul') in 1861 in honor of Grand Duke Paul Alexandrovich of Russia (1860–1919).
b_pavlodar.etymology_analysis: Russian compound meaning 'Gift of Paul', bestowed in 1861 to commemorate the birth of Grand Duke Paul Alexandrovich.

b_tatarki.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; ethnonymic Russian plural form (Tatarki) associated with the Pavlodar/Irtysh region.
b_tatarki.etymology_analysis: Russian ethnonym-derived plural settlement name based on Tatar.

b_yamishevo.first_mention_attestation: Founded in October–November 1715 as Yamyshevskaya fortress on the Irtysh River by Ivan Buchholz's expedition in Pavlodar Region, Kazakhstan.
b_yamishevo.etymology_analysis: Russian settlement name with the -evo suffix derived from nearby salt lake Yamyshevskoye (Yamysh).

b_koriakovsky.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1720 as the Koryakovsky military outpost on the Irtysh Line (predecessor of Pavlodar), named after nearby Lake Koryakovskoye.
b_koriakovsky.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival outpost name (-sky) derived from nearby salt lake Koryakovskoye.

b_bardak.first_mention_attestation: First documented in Russian sources in 1594 during the subjugation of the Principality of Bardak (Bardakovo) near Surgut.
b_bardak.eponym_details: Named after the late-16th-century Khanty chieftain Bardak (fl. 1594).
b_bardak.etymology_analysis: Named after the indigenous Khanty ruler Prince Bardak, whose fortified settlement near Surgut was conquered by Muscovy in 1594.

b_berisiy.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name.
b_berisiy.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for Western Siberia; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name.

b_yorgaet.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name.
b_yorgaet.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for Western Siberia; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name.

b_demiianka.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Demyanka River and settlement in Tyumen and Omsk oblasts.
b_demiianka.etymology_analysis: Named after the Demyanka River, a major right tributary of the Irtysh.

b_selinga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or misplaced CK3 barony name in Belogorye.

morphemes.translation: Unattested in Western Siberia (cf. Selenga River in Buryatia)

b_selinga.etymology_analysis: No settlement or river named Selinga is attested in the Ob–Irtysh Belogorye region; likely a misplaced or synthetic CK3 name.

b_sibir.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Siberian Tatar fortress of Sibir (Qashliq/Isker) near Tobolsk is first attested in 1367 CE as Sebur on the Pizzigani brothers' map and in 14th-century Russian chronicles.

morphemes.translation: Fortress and historical region of Sibir (etymology debated)

b_sibir.etymology_analysis: Medieval fortress (also called Qashliq or Isker) on the Irtysh near Tobolsk and eponymous choronym of Siberia, first attested in 14th-century Russian chronicles.

b_asmaak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name in Sibir.
b_asmaak.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for Western Siberia; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name.

b_vagaiskoy.first_mention_attestation: Russian adjectival form (Vagayskoye) of Vagay in Tyumen Oblast, founded in 1633.
b_vagaiskoy.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival settlement form (-skoy/-skoye) derived from the Vagay River.

b_tobol.first_mention_attestation: Tobolsk was founded in 1587 by Cossacks under Danilo Chulkov at the confluence of the Tobol and Irtysh rivers, named after the Tobol River.
b_tobol.etymology_analysis: Hydronym of the Tobol River, a major left tributary of the Irtysh, which gave its name to Tobolsk (founded 1587).

b_koshley_vosh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name.
b_koshley_vosh.etymology_analysis: Appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name combining an unattested stem with Khanty vosh ('town/fortress').

b_uluskate.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name.
b_uluskate.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical sources; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name incorporating Turkic/Mongolic ulus.

b_liniek.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name.
b_liniek.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for Western Siberia; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name.

b_chich.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; corresponds to the Late Bronze/Early Iron Age archaeological site of Chicha-1 (9th–7th c. BCE) on Lake Malaya Chicha in Novosibirsk Oblast, which lacks contemporary written records.

morphemes.translation: Modern toponym of Lake Malaya Chicha and the Chicha-1 site

b_chich.etymology_analysis: Modern name of Lake Malaya Chicha and the prehistoric Chicha-1 fortified settlement (9th–7th c. BCE) in the Baraba steppe, without pre-867 written attestation.

b_olyn.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; synthetic or unattested CK3 barony name.
b_olyn.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or geographic sources for Western Siberia; appears to be a synthetic CK3 barony name.

b_kargalin.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; documented in 19th-century Russian administrative records of Kargalinskaya Volost, Tarsky Uyezd, Tobolsk Governorate.
b_kargalin.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival settlement form derived from the Turkic toponym Kargaly/Kargala, historically a volost center in Tarsky Uyezd (modern Vikulovsky District, Tyumen Oblast).

b_kazanskoye.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1758 CE as a Russian frontier settlement on the Alabuga River in southern Tyumen Oblast.

morphemes.translation: Kazan (referring to the Virgin of Kazan / Kazan)

b_kazanskoye.etymology_analysis: Russian neuter adjectival settlement name derived from Kazan (typically via a church dedicated to Our Lady of Kazan); founded in 1758 CE.

b_tenis.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after Lake Tenis in Omsk Oblast, documented only in modern Russian geographical records.
b_tenis.etymology_analysis: Hydronym from Lake Tenis in the West Siberian Plain (Omsk Oblast), derived from Siberian Tatar teŋiz ('sea, large lake').

b_tukalinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1759 CE as the post station Tyukalinsky Stanets on the Tyukala River along the Siberian Route.
b_tukalinsk.etymology_analysis: Russian town name with the -insk suffix formed from the Tyukala River hydronym; established in 1759 CE as a postal station and granted town status in 1823 CE.

b_petropavolsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1752 CE as the Russian military fortress of Petropavlovsk on the Ishim River.
b_petropavolsk.etymology_analysis: Russian fortress name (CK3 spelling petropavolsk for Petropavlovsk, modern Kazakh Petropavl) named after the 1st-century CE Apostles Saints Peter and Paul, founded in 1752 CE.

b_sargatka.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1764 CE as a Russian settlement on the Sargatka River in Omsk Oblast.
b_sargatka.etymology_analysis: Colloquial Russian settlement name Sargatka (official form Sargatskoye), derived from the Sargatka River; founded in 1764 CE.

b_ibeitei.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name in the Irtysh/Omsk region.
b_ibeitei.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or modern gazetteers; treated as a synthetic or obscure CK3 barony name in d_tara.

b_tara.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1594 CE as the first permanent Russian fortified settlement in the Omsk region, at the confluence of the Tara and Irtysh rivers.
b_tara.etymology_analysis: Named directly after the Tara River (a right tributary of the Irtysh); the Russian town was founded in 1594 CE.

b_zavialova.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1730 CE (also cited as 1736 CE in local records) as a Russian settler village in Znamensky District, Omsk Oblast.
b_zavialova.eponym_details: Named after an 18th-century Russian settler/founder with the surname Zavyalov.
b_zavialova.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive village name (Zavyalova / Zavyalovo) derived from the personal surname Zavyalov; founded in 1730 CE.

b_kulema.first_mention_attestation: Attested on Guillaume Delisle's 1706 CE map as Kulema/Kulemba along the Om/Irtysh region; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kulema.etymology_analysis: Historical 17th–18th-century Siberian settlement name appearing on Delisle's 1706 CE map in the Om/Tara region.

b_kartaszevo.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1719 CE as a Russian village on the Irtysh route between Tara and Omsk (modern Muromtsevsky District, Omsk Oblast).
b_kartaszevo.eponym_details: Named after an early 18th-century Russian settler/founder with the surname or nickname Kartash / Kartashev.
b_kartaszevo.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive village name (CK3 spelling kartaszevo for Kartashevo) from the surname Kartashev; founded around 1719 CE.

b_surgut.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1594 CE by order of Tsar Feodor I as a Russian fortress on the Ob River near an Ostyak (Khanty) settlement.
b_surgut.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of a Khanty toponym (commonly linked to Khanty words for 'floodplain' and 'fish'); the Russian fort was founded in 1594 CE.

b_khanty-mansiisk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1931 CE as the workers' settlement of Ostyako-Vogulsk and renamed Khanty-Mansiysk in 1940 CE (absorbing nearby Samarovo, first attested in 1582 CE).
b_khanty-mansiisk.etymology_analysis: Soviet-era ethnonymic town name (1940 CE, replacing Ostyako-Vogulsk founded 1931 CE) honoring the indigenous Khanty and Mansi peoples.

b_yugan.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; named after the Bolshoy Yugan River in Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, documented in post-16th-century Russian sources.
b_yugan.etymology_analysis: Hydronym from the Bolshoy Yugan / Maly Yugan rivers, derived from Khanty jŏɣan ('river').

b_nizyani.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; historical Khanty settlement of the Koda Principality documented in 16th–18th-century Russian sources.
b_nizyani.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of the Northern Khanty settlement name Nizyam (CK3 spelling nizyani), a historic fortified settlement of the Koda Principality on the Ob River.

b_atlym.first_mention_attestation: Founded or first attested in 1592 CE in Russian records as a Khanty settlement of the Koda Principality along the Ob River.
b_atlym.etymology_analysis: Historic Northern Khanty settlement name (Atlym / Bolshoy and Maly Atlym) in the Koda Principality, first documented in Russian sources in 1592 CE.

b_karymkary.first_mention_attestation: First written mention dates to 1581 CE in Russian accounts of the lower Ob and Koda Principality.

morphemes.translation: sterlet / fish-related or local clan root

b_karymkary.etymology_analysis: Ob-Ugric settlement name in Oktyabrsky District (Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug), first recorded in Russian written sources in 1581 CE.

b_sukhorukova.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; former Russian village in Khanty-Mansiysky District documented in 18th–20th-century archival records before its early-21st-century abolition.
b_sukhorukova.eponym_details: Named after an early Russian settler with the surname or nickname Sukhorukov ('dry-handed').
b_sukhorukova.etymology_analysis: Russian possessive village name (Sukhorukova / Sukhorukovo) from the surname Sukhorukov, located near Khanty-Mansiysk until its abolition in 2011 CE.

b_belogorye.first_mention_attestation: Documented in connection with Yermak's 1582 CE campaign on the Ob-Irtysh confluence and later in Grigori Novitsky's 1715 CE account.
b_belogorye.etymology_analysis: Russian descriptive toponym meaning 'white hills', applied to a settlement and sacred Ob-Ugrian site near the Ob-Irtysh confluence; attested from 1582 CE.

b_kartauzh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; historical center of the Mansi Konda Principality (Kondia) documented in 16th-century Russian sources.
b_kartauzh.etymology_analysis: Ob-Ugric fortified settlement name (Russian Kartauzh) serving as the capital of the late-medieval Mansi Konda Principality (conquered by Muscovy in 1593–1594 CE).

b_kandiskaya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1847 CE as a Russian settlement in Kondinsky District, Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug.
b_kandiskaya.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival settlement form (CK3 kandiskaya for Kondinskaya / Kondinskoye) derived from the Konda River; founded in 1847 CE.

b_kharam-vosh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ob-Ugric toponym recorded only in post-medieval ethnographic and historical literature.
b_kharam-vosh.etymology_analysis: Ob-Ugric settlement name containing the element -vosh ('town, fortified settlement'), located in the Konda basin.

b_kari_pospat_vosh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; legendary Khanty fortified town (Karį-pôspat vos) recorded in 19th-century Ostyak/Khanty heroic epic folklore.
b_kari_pospat_vosh.etymology_analysis: Legendary Khanty fortified town (Karį-pôspat vos) known from Patkanov's 19th-century collection of Ostyak heroic epics.

b_arant.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested or obscure CK3 barony name in the Konda region.
b_arant.etymology_analysis: Unattested in documented <= 867 CE or standard modern Russian/Ob-Ugric gazetteers; used as a CK3 barony in d_konda.

b_tselym_dalyn.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; obscure Ob-Ugric or CK3 barony name in the Konda basin.
b_tselym_dalyn.etymology_analysis: Obscure Ob-Ugric or CK3-adapted barony name in d_konda with no pre-867 CE written attestation.

b_chukas_vosh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; historical Ob-Ugric gorodok (-vosh) documented only in post-medieval Siberian ethnographic and historical works.
b_chukas_vosh.etymology_analysis: Ob-Ugric fortified settlement name with -vosh ('town, fortified settlement'), appearing in historical lists of Yugran gorodki.

b_topar_vosh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; historical Ob-Ugric gorodok (-vosh) documented only in post-medieval Siberian ethnographic and historical works.
b_topar_vosh.etymology_analysis: Ob-Ugric fortified settlement name with -vosh ('town, fortified settlement'), appearing in historical lists of Yugran gorodki.

b_laia.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1726 CE by Russian settlers from the Kerzhenets River on the Laya River in Sverdlovsk Oblast (nearby Malaya Laya founded 1684 CE).
b_laia.etymology_analysis: Named after the Laya River (a tributary of the Tagil); the village of Laya in Sverdlovsk Oblast was founded in 1726 CE.

b_tagil.first_mention_attestation: Iron ore mining began in 1696 CE (followed by ironworks and permanent settlement in 1722 CE) along the Tagil River in Sverdlovsk Oblast.
b_tagil.etymology_analysis: Hydronym from the Tagil River (variously derived from Mansi or Turkic roots), giving its name to Nizhny Tagil (mining from 1696 CE, ironworks 1722 CE).

b_deriabinskoye.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1680 CE in Verkhotursky District, Sverdlovsk Oblast.
b_deriabinskoye.eponym_details: Named after the 17th-century Russian Cossack/settler Fyodor Deryaba.
b_deriabinskoye.etymology_analysis: Russian adjectival settlement name (Deryabinskoye / modern Deryabino) named after its 1680 CE founder Fyodor Deryaba.

b_neramkary.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; historical Ob-Ugric fortified settlement (-kary) documented only in post-medieval Siberian historical lists.
b_neramkary.etymology_analysis: Ob-Ugric fortified settlement name with -kary ('town, fortress'), attested in post-medieval Siberian historical geography.

b_verkhoturye.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1598 CE as a Russian ostrog (fort) on the upper Tura River along Babinov's route into Siberia.
b_verkhoturye.etymology_analysis: Russian locator compound meaning 'upper Tura' (founded 1598 CE on the upper reaches of the Tura River).

b_tabary.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1594 CE as a Russian fort by Prince Pyotr Gorchakov on the site of the Mansi Tabary volost.

morphemes.translation: local Mansi/Tatar tribal or settlement name (Tabary)

b_tabary.etymology_analysis: Russian adaptation of the Mansi/Tatar settlement and volost name Tabary (modern Tabory, Sverdlovsk Oblast), where a fort was built in 1594 CE.

b_tura_kala.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Turkic-Siberian compound name unattested in pre-867 CE written sources.
b_tura_kala.etymology_analysis: Compound of Siberian Turkic tura ('town/fortress' or Tura River) and kala ('fortress'), with no <= 867 CE written attestation.

b_oblacas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name in d_ostyaki.
b_oblacas.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or modern gazetteers; treated as a synthetic or garbled CK3 barony name in c_tabary.

b_tyumen.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1586 CE as the first Russian city in Siberia on the site of the Siberian Tatar town of Chimgi-Tura (12th–16th centuries CE).
b_tyumen.etymology_analysis: Derived from Turkic-Mongolic tümen ('ten thousand', a military-administrative division); refounded by Russia in 1586 CE over medieval Chimgi-Tura.

b_terom.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested or synthetic CK3 barony name in c_tyumen.
b_terom.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or modern Siberian gazetteers; treated as a synthetic or obscure CK3 barony name.

b_turinsk.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1600 CE as a Russian ostrog on the site of the Tatar town of Yepanchin (razed by Yermak in 1581 CE).
b_turinsk.etymology_analysis: Russian town name with the -insk suffix formed from the Tura River; founded in 1600 CE on the site of Yepanchin.

b_shantoskoye.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested or synthetic CK3 Russian-suffixed barony name in c_tyumen.
b_shantoskoye.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or modern gazetteers; synthetic or garbled CK3 barony using the Russian -skoye settlement suffix.

b_koshuki.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; late 16th-century Vogul (Mansi) settlement mentioned in N. M. Karamzin's History of the Russian State.
b_koshuki.eponym_details: Named after Koshuk Araslanov, a late 16th-century Bashkir/Tatar leader of the local Vogul (Mansi) yurts.
b_koshuki.etymology_analysis: Russian pluralized settlement name derived from the late 16th-century leader Koshuk Araslanov (modern village of Koshuki in Tavdinsky District, Sverdlovsk Oblast).

b_alymka.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in Lev Poskochin's 1681–1683 CE census of Tobolsk Uyezd as a settlement on the Alymka River.
b_alymka.etymology_analysis: Named after the Alymka River in Uvatsky District, Tyumen Oblast; first attested in the 1681–1683 CE Tobolsk Uyezd census.

b_chalbych.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested or obscure CK3 barony name in c_koshuki.
b_chalbych.etymology_analysis: Unattested in historical or modern gazetteers; treated as a synthetic or obscure CK3 barony name in d_pelym.

b_pelym.first_mention_attestation: Russian fort built in 1592 CE by Prince Pyotr Gorchakov on the site of the Mansi Pelym Principality's center at the Pelym River.
b_pelym.etymology_analysis: Named after the Pelym River (Mansi Polum); the Russian fort of Pelym was established in 1592 CE.

b_sosva.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Sosva River is documented in 16th-century Russian and European accounts, and the modern settlement in Sverdlovsk Oblast is post-medieval.
b_sosva.etymology_analysis: Named after the Sosva River (a tributary of the Tavda in Sverdlovsk Oblast), from an indigenous Mansi/Komi hydronym.

b_totkarak.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; unattested or obscure CK3 barony name in c_pelym.
b_totkarak.etymology_analysis: Unattested in documented <= 867 CE or standard modern Russian/Ob-Ugric gazetteers; used as a CK3 barony in d_pelym.
